newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels say they set to capture diamond town.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels say they set to capture diamond town.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila has said his forces will soon capture the diamond mining centre of Mbuji-Mayi, knocking down reports the town had already fallen.
"We are going forward, we are advancing and we are not far less than 10 km (six miles) from Mbuji-Mayi and in the vicinity of Lubumbashi," Kabila told a news conference late on Friday.
Earlier reports by mining sources in Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city, said the rebels had marched into Mbuji-Mayi after government troops went on a looting spree and fled to nearby Kananga.
Kabila's rebel forces, who have seized more than a fifth of the vast Central African country since last October, pose a grave threat to President Mobutu Sese Seko's hold on power.
Mobutu has ruled Zaire since 1965 but is now ailing with cancer.

The rebellion began when Banyamulenge Tutsis took up arms in October to fight attempts by Zairean authorities to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda. The rebel fold has expanded to include other Mobutu opponents determined to topple him.

Senior officials of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire (AFDL) have said privately the capture of either Mbuji-Mayi or Kananga would be timed to coincide with the start of peace talks between the government and the rebels in South Africa.
The two sides were due to meet face-to-face for the first time on Saturday but prospects for any quick ceasefire looked bleak.
The talks were to start at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT) at the South African government's main headquarters in Pretoria.
Mobutu's security adviser and chairman of the eight-member government negotiating team, Honore Ngbanda, arrived in South Africa on Thursday ahead of Kabila's envoy Bizima Karaha.
Kabila has shrugged off all offers so far from Kinshasa, insisting that only the removal of Mobutu would satisfy his rebel movement.
"There is no problem with the ceasefire. All we need is for the Alliance to ascend to power," he said.
Kabila criticised the United Nations over its refugee policy and condemned a U.N. human rights report on alleged abuses in rebel territory.
"We are...sick to death of the unjust treatment of the international community and especially the UNHCR (U.N. refugee agency)," he said.

The agency was pursuing a hidden agenda of creating new refugee camps south of rebel-held Kisangani while failing to credit his alliance with facilitating the return home of more than half million Rwandan Hutus last November.
"These are the lies presented to the world by the UNHCR," Kabila said.
Around 80,000 Hutu refugees are stranded in desperate conditions south of Kisangani, Zaire's third city, and aid workers say the rebels are blocking a plan to repatriate them.

More than one million refugees, including members of the former Rwandan government army and extremist militiamen who played a leading role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, fled camps in Zaire's Kivu region last year at the start of the rebel campaign.
The rebels said the U.N. human rights report alleging widespread massacres in rebel-held territory was baseless and an insult to the international community.
The U.N. had "no right to peddle these disgusting lies in front of the international community in the hope of discrediting the AFDL," the rebels said in a statement.
